text:
I want to write a request for promotion to senior paralegal. I've been a paralegal in the litigation group of a 60-lawyer law firm for 5 years.

Facts:
- I support 4 lawyers and worked on 23 cases last year, including 2 that went to trial.
- I built the group's tracking sheet for court deadlines in 2023. Two other groups in the firm now use it.
- Last March I entered a filing deadline wrong in that same sheet. Another paralegal noticed, and we filed 2 hours before the court's cutoff. After that I added a second-person check to the sheet.
- I billed 1,640 hours last year. The group's target is 1,550.
- I trained the 3 paralegals the group hired in the last 2 years.
- A senior paralegal is paid $9,000 a year more and supervises the other paralegals.

Keep it under 400 words. It goes to the managing partner of our group.

Before I draft this, a few questions. Your answers would change what the letter says:

1. **Is there an opening right now?** Is the senior paralegal role vacant, newly created, or would your promotion mean the group has two seniors? If someone already holds the role, the partner's first thought will be "why do we need another one?"
2. **Does the partner already know about the March deadline error?** If they do, I'd raise it briefly and stress the second-person check you added, since that is a supervisory fix. If they don't, tell me whether you want it in the letter at all.
3. **Have you already been supervising anyone informally?** For example, reviewing the new paralegals' work, assigning tasks, or answering their questions after training ended. Supervision is the main new duty in the senior role, so any proof that you already do it is the strongest point you have.
4. **Is there anything a lawyer would say for you?** Could one of the 4 lawyers you support back the request, or did either trial go especially well because of your work? Even one line of praise from a lawyer helps.
5. **What are you asking for, and by when?** Is it the title plus the $9,000, starting at a particular date such as the next review cycle or January? Do you want a meeting? Also give me the partner's name and how you want to sign off.
6. **Is there anything the partner knows or will find out that the facts above leave out?** For example, a prior promotion request that was turned down, a performance review comment, or someone more senior who also wants the role.

If you don't know some of these, just say so. I'll write without them and won't guess.

1. I don't know.
2. I don't know if he knows. Keep it in, but don't say I'll never make an error again, I can't promise that. Since the second-person check went in last April, the sheet has had no wrong or missed deadlines in about 600 entries.
3. I don't know beyond the training.
4. I don't know.
5. The title and the $9,000. Promotions are decided in the January review cycle, and requests are due December 15. I'd like to meet with him in person to talk about it. His name is David Kessler. Sign it Jenna Morales.
6. One of the 3 paralegals I trained left after 8 months. Also, if I get the role I can commit to running a short weekly check-in with the paralegals I'd supervise, and to finishing the state paralegal certification by next June.

I've drafted the letter at about 300 words. A few notes on the choices I made:

- **The March error:** The letter says plainly what happened and then gives the 600 error-free entries since the check went in. It doesn't promise you'll never make another mistake. Instead it says you build systems that catch mistakes before they reach a court.
- **The paralegal who left:** David will probably know about this already, so the letter says it plainly and doesn't guess why they left. Your weekly check-in comes right after it. That shows how you'd supervise without claiming the check-ins would have changed anything.
- **The meeting:** You're asking to meet before the December 15 deadline, which leaves time to talk before requests are due.
- **What would make it stronger:** If a lawyer you support would vouch for you, or you've been checking the newer paralegals' work beyond training, one sentence on either would strengthen the supervision case.

Subject: Request for promotion to Senior Paralegal

Dear David,

I'm writing to ask to be considered for promotion to Senior Paralegal in the January review cycle. I'm requesting the title and the $9,000 salary increase that comes with it.

I have been a paralegal in the litigation group for five years. Last year I supported four lawyers across 23 cases, two of which went to trial, and billed 1,640 hours against the group's target of 1,550.

The senior role means supervising the other paralegals, and I already do some of that work. I trained all three paralegals the group has hired in the last two years. Two are still with us, and one left after eight months.

In 2023 I built the group's court-deadline tracking sheet. Two other groups in the firm have since adopted it. Last March I entered a filing deadline wrong in that sheet. Another paralegal caught the error, and we filed two hours before the court's cutoff. That was too close. In April I added a second-person check to every entry. Since then the sheet has recorded about 600 deadlines, and none has been wrong or missed. I can't promise I'll never make a mistake. I can promise to build systems that catch mistakes, mine or anyone else's, before they reach a court. That is the work I would bring to the senior role.

If promoted, I commit to two things:

- Running a short weekly check-in with the paralegals I supervise, so that questions and problems come up early.
- Completing the state paralegal certification by June 2027.

I would like to discuss this with you in person before requests are due on December 15. Please let me know a time that works for you.

Thank you for considering my request.

Best regards,
Jenna Morales
